title: The Scorpion Gesture
description: "For The Scorpion Gesture, Chitra Ganesh created a series of animated artistic interventions in the Rubin’s collection galleries. All five are inspired by nearby artworks that relate to Padmasabhava, known to Tibetans as the Second Buddha, and Maitreya, the Future Buddha, though each departs from the aesthetics and iconography associated with the traditional works. Ganesh’s animations reveal her inimitable and brilliant skill of translating complex narratives—often of mythological or epic proportion—into poetic, contemporary, and lucid visual stories. While this approach is also evident in her paintings and drawings, it is further amplified in her animations," --Beth Citron, Curator
creator: Chitra Ganesh
item-description: Collages of line drawings, watercolors, and paintings to currate animations

title: The Scorpion Gesture, Rainbow Body
description: "The title of this work refers to an elevated state of, or metaphor for, the consciousness transformation known as a rainbow body. The Buddhist master Padmasambhava achieved this state from his union with Mandarava, a female spirit (dakini) and princess in Tantric Buddhism. Through study and physical connection, each played a key role in the other’s enlightenment. Rainbow Body takes inspiration from the cave on the right in the painting of the bodhisattva Maitreya, located adjacent to the animation. The cave structure is elaborated upon and extensively built out, introducing an interior depth where the ultimate transformation happens. I wanted to work with a narrative structure of dreamlike density, moving the viewer through a succession of physical and psychic spaces. The animation opens with Mandarava waking up to a dream in her bedroom and follows her journey through the bardo, the sometimes terrifying passageway between death and rebirth. The aerial and gliding camera movements reconfigure imagery of the bardo from paintings with a greater sense of space and depth. The work also combines my line drawings, watercolors, and paintings with pictorial elements from a variety of original sources," —Chitra Ganesh
creator: Chitra Ganesh
item-description: Collages of line drawings, watercolors, and paintings to currate animations

title: The Scorpion Gesture, Sillouette in the Graveyard
description: This animation involved a challenging set of constraints: developing and presenting a moving-image work with a collection object in the frame. The sculpture of the bodhisattva Maitreya is positioned at the front and center of the animation, and it therefore informed artistic decisions regarding imagery, composition, and narrative progression. Maitreya is the Future Buddha, whose prophetic arrival is said to usher in a new age at a time when the terrestrial world has lost its way. The endless stream of images of political, social, and ecological upheaval that we are bombarded with daily seemed in uncanny alignment with the apocalyptic moment associated with Maitreya. Negotiating the spatial relations between the object and my own work inspired a more experimental narrative approach, with references to theater and the performative nature of protest shaping my treatment of photographic and video material. The river of blood gestures to the liminal space between life and death that is a recurring trope in this series of animations. ---Chitra Ganesh
creator: Chitra Ganesh
item-description: Collages of line drawings, watercolors, and paintings to currate animations

title: The Unknowns, Skype in Real Time
description: "The Unknowns explores the relationship between anonymity, mass-mediated images, and the monumental, in the construction of a feminine iconography. Ganesh collages and appropriates materials from divergent sources, including 1960s-70s B-grade movies, 19th century orientalist painting, documentary photography of sex workers and mid-century studio photography in India. Sculptural elements, extracted from objects of daily life (shower curtains, fake hair, automotive glass, etc), suggest an entangling of the mythic feminine and everyday material culture." --Chitra Ganesh's website

title: she always charges my hearing aids for me so i listen to her
description: "The biggest way that my work has shifted over the last few years has been through my experience with hearing loss, which has been progressive. In the past, my videos were almost always me talking to camera, creating an illusion. But as my ability to mix the sound properly has become more difficult, I’ve been doing more speech-free videos, where they fully rely on visual language. This has created such a special impact,  pushing me so much further in both my video and physical practices!" --Kari on the influence of sound in her art

title: Berry Baskets
description: "By age twenty they became the youngest person to receive the title of master basket maker, using ash and sweetgrass they prepare themselves to weave vibrant narratives combining Wabanaki teachings with their own perspectives.  Their signature style — whimsical, sculptural, and rooted in Passamaquoddy tradition — weaves ancestral knowledge and two-spirit identity into every form, making baskets that are simultaneously cultural preservation and personal testimony," --Tim Tate, Sculptor

item-description: Six woven green and purple baskets joined together on a "vine," shaped like berries

title: Basket With Color
description: “My grandmother, her mother, and her mother all wove their Strawberry baskets on the same form, and in the same style. Eventually, my grandmother promised the mold which the berries are woven on to me, in order to carry on her family's Strawberry style. Until I received the mold, I had only woven "unripe" or partially red berries--a symbol that, as her apprentice, I was still a growing berry, and my Grandmother, my teacher, and best friend was the fully grown, ripened red Strawberry,” --Geo Soctomah Neptune
creator: Geo Neptune
item-description: One large basket with a straw handle, pink-red in color to resemble a strawberry

title: Dinner Party
description: "Judy Chicago’s The Dinner Party (1974–79) is an icon of 1970s American feminist art, one of the most important artworks of the 20th century, and a visitor favorite. The large-scale installation celebrates the lives and achievements of historical and mythical women across Western civilization in the form of a lavish banquet table set for 39. The names of 999 more women stream out on the Heritage Floor. Conceptually daring and visually dazzling, Chicago’s landmark artwork challenges centuries of patriarchal erasure of women’s history. This feat is executed in brilliant detail across the painted and shaped ceramic plates and richly embellished needlework runners, materials specifically chosen for their resonance with so-called women’s work," --Brooklyn Museum
creator: Judy Chicago
item-description: Large triangular black table, with different place settings to represent different feminist artists

title: Dinner Party
description: "Once derided as “3-D ceramic pornography” by a U.S. congressman, The Dinner Party’s symbolic layers reward close looking. They focus on the “central core” (or vulvar) imagery in an unprecedented embrace of body-based abstract art that was highly controversial in the years following its debut. Despite the critics, The Dinner Party was always beloved, attracting droves of visitors eager to see women’s history fully celebrated. The gift of this work to the Brooklyn Museum created the Center for Feminist Art, where the installation is on permanent display and surrounded by rotating galleries of feminist art," --Brooklyn Museum
creator: Judy Chicago
item-description: Large triangular black table, with different place settings to represent different feminist artists

title: MOMENTATIONAL SCENT CHAMBER  I and II
description: "In the upstairs gallery, Adam Farah-Saad presents a floor-based grid of prints beneath liquid-filled perspex trays, collectively imaging two men in bondage. On two opposing walls, a pair of box frames or ‘scent chambers’ house sliding panels of reeded perspex and C-type prints mounted on aluminum, through which complementary olfactory works formulated by the artist diffuse into the space. While Farah-Saad has explored olfactory dimensions within his practice for nearly a decade, particularly in relation to psychogeography, queer sociality and gentrification, this new body of work marks a shift into self-formulated fragrance. He presents two conceptual scents: NW1 (2025), carrying notes of fresh cut grass, petitgrain, tonka and birch tar; and W9 (2025), with notes of vetiver, guaiacwood, cypriol, herbal smoke, orris, musk and warm skin. Together, they recall a memory of a summer evening in 2020 which began in Primrose Hill and ended at a romantic partner’s flat in Maida Vale, forming a vessel for his memory to unfold, a portal into the atmosphere of a relationship and the traces it leaves behind," --Public Gallery
creator: Adam Farah-Saad

title: The Scent of Skin
description:
"Huang Zejian is a multidisciplinary artist working across sculpture, installation, photography, digital painting, printmaking, and drawing. His practice centers on the body as a site where desire, intimacy, and information intersect.
Using amorphous forms constructed from mixed materials and nylon fabric, Huang creates sculptural works that evoke the visceral allure of the human body—particularly limbs—transforming them into fluid, ambiguous structures that oscillate between sensuality and vulnerability. These organic forms blur the boundary between abstraction and corporeality, suggesting the instability of identity and desire," --Zejian's Artsy Listing
creator: Huang Zejian
item-description: White room with both bodily sculptures, No. 87 and 88 hung up on opposite walls

title: The Scent of Skin, No. 87
description: "In this soft sculpture, Huang Zejian fragments images of human skin and reconstructs them through satin, stitching, and volume into an unfamiliar bodily form. Detached from their original anatomy, recognizable traces of skin, limbs, folds, and intimate surfaces overlap and migrate across the sculpture, making it impossible to locate a single, coherent body... Suspended between abstraction and physical intimacy, the sculpture becomes less a representation of a particular person than a composite body: sensual, unstable, and strangely alive. Huang uses skin as both image and material language, exploring how bodily memory persists even after identity and anatomical order have disappeared," --Zejin's Artsy Listing
creator: Huang Zejian
item-description: Phallic satin sculpture of various pink, burgundy, and tan shapes

title: The Scent of Skin, No. 88
description: "In Scent of Skin, Huang treats skin as both image and interface—a surface through which intimacy, desire, memory, and our perception of others are formed. No. 88 becomes a body without a fixed identity: fragmented and reconstructed, yet strangely tender and alive," --Zejin's Artsy Listing
creator: Huang Zejian
item-description: Vaginal satin sculpture of various teal, brown, and tan shapes
